hints: k can be as large as 109, but rotating n times brings the array back to where it started. What does that tell you about k?

First reduce k = k % n. Then use the reversal trick on nums: reverse the whole array, reverse the first k elements, reverse the remaining n − k. This rotates in place, and the function returns nothing.

approaches.name: Brute force
approaches.idea: Move the array one step right, k times.

approaches.name: Better
approaches.idea: Copy each nums[i] into a new array at position (i + k) % n, then copy it back.

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.idea: Three reversals (whole, first k, rest) after reducing k modulo n.

explain: For nums = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] with k = 2: reversing everything gives [5, 4, 3, 2, 1], reversing the first two gives [4, 5, 3, 2, 1], reversing the last three gives [4, 5, 1, 2, 3]. The last k elements need to move to the front, and the full reversal puts them there (backwards), so the two smaller reversals fix the order inside each block. Always take k % n first, otherwise huge k values break the indices; k % n = 0 leaves the array unchanged.
recognize: "Rotate by k steps" with large k → reduce k mod n, then the three-reversal trick (or index math).
